title: In whole-brain spiking models from FlyWire and male CNS fly connectomes, the same taste neuron types can drive feeding motor neuron MN9, but the necessary drive differs by map and body side
abstract: Question: does the Shiu et al. 2024 whole-brain leaky integrate-and-fire model of the fly make the same feeding prediction (taste input drives proboscis motor neuron MN9) when it is built from a second connectome, and from the other body side? Approach: a numba re-implementation (neuron-level r = 0.999 against the original Brian2 code) built from FlyWire v783 and the Janelia male CNS v1.0. We drove all neurons of 8 labellar taste types and 6 other sensory types per side at 50 to 200 Hz, with the published weight (FlyWire) and an input-matched and an MN9-calibrated weight (male CNS). Results: in both maps only sugar LB3c, salt LB3d, LB3b and LB4a-b drove MN9 above 10 Hz; water LB3a, bitter, LB1e and LB2 never did (68 non-ignited runs, maximum 3.3 Hz). The necessary drive was not robust: left FlyWire sugar neurons gave 61 Hz at 100 Hz input, right ones 0 Hz; male CNS left 0 Hz, right 7 Hz. FlyWire left LB3 taste neurons have 2.2 to 3.4 times more output synapses than the right ones. Synaptic dose (rate x weight x output synapses) predicted MN9 better than rate (AIC 81 vs 119), but map and side terms still helped (AIC 72). In the male map, MN9 activation starts at w 0.175 to 0.19 mV and global runaway at 0.21 to 0.225 mV. Whole-brain type-level responses agreed less between maps (cosine 0.38) than between sides (0.63, 0.79; p = 0.002). The original Shiu water set contains 7 sugar LB3c neurons; its LB3a part alone gives no MN9. Limitations: model results only; two flies of different sex and pipeline; one global weight per map; incomplete right MN9 in male CNS.
